newsitem.title: ALBANIA: New right-wing party emerges from Albanian crisis.
newsitem.headline: New right-wing party emerges from Albanian crisis.

text.p: A splinter right-wing party pledging to restore law and order emerged on Saturday from Albania's political and social chaos of recent months.

The Movement for Democracy (MDP) was formed by a group of politicans who broke away from President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, which has won the last two of three general elections since the fall of communism in 1990 ended 46 years of Albanian isolation and hardline Stalinist rule.

Parliamentarian Dashamir Shehi, a founder of the Democratic Party, said the MDP had the support of 14 of the 140 members of parliament but hoped to form an alliance with other right and centre parties for a general election expected on June 29.
"This movement is a product of the general crisis in Albania and the general crisis in the Democratic Party," Shehi told a news conference.
"The core of the programme is stability, restoration of law and order and proper goverment for Albania."

Shehi said there had been underlying tension in Albania since the last election in May 1996 which opposition Socialists boycotted amid charges of intimidation and vote-rigging. International monitors described the polling as seriously flawed.

When five get-rich-quick "pyramid" schemes collapsed in January, losing thousands of people's savings, Albanians took to the streets, raiding state arsenals and creating near-anarchy with more than 300 people killed in the violence.
Armed rebels, who blame Berisha for the pyramid scheme disaster, still control much of southern Albania.
"The whole Albanian crisis in general had a culmination point in the pyramid schemes," Shehi said.
"It was the responsibility of the Democratic Party...to give a solution for this but this did not happen.
"But we must now make it clear to the Albanian population that the amount of money lost in the Albanian roulette (estimated at $1.2 billion) is almost impossible to return."

Shehi said that to restore law and order, Albania needed to reorganise its army and police force, detaching these groups from politics, gain broader international support, but, above all, provide a stable, respected government.
"After the election there will be a stable government supported by the parliament and that is our main aim," he said.
Albania is currently led by an interim all-party government that was appointed on March 11 to calm the country and to prepare for fresh parliamentary elections in June three years ahead of schedule.
A five-member European Democratic Union (EDU) mission met leaders of the Democratic Party, the Socialists, Berisha and Prime Minister Bashkim Fino on Friday and Saturday.

"We're here to bring our solidarity to the people of Albania...and also to bring our friendship for the Democratic Party of Albania," mission leader Jose Maria Robles Fraga, international secretary of the People's Party of Spain, told a news conference on Saturday.
"The prospect of elections and elections themselves are crucial. We hope the dialogue can be kept going on all aspects that are under controversy, including the election law.
"From our point of view there would be no excuse for breaking the spirit of dialogue and for breaking the authority of democratically elected local authorities."
